sources.name: location.hash
sources.explain: The URL fragment (everything after #), fully attacker-controlled by crafting a link. Read via location.hash or window.location.hash.substring(1).
sources.notes: The fragment is NEVER sent to the server — server-side WAFs and access logs are blind to it. Always URL-encode the payload properly in the PoC link; browsers keep the fragment through redirects.

sources.name: location.search
sources.explain: The query string (?a=b&c=d), attacker-controlled via a crafted link and readable directly or through parsers.
sources.notes: Unlike the fragment, the query string IS sent to the server — so a server-side WAF may strip or block obvious payloads; try encoding variants, or prefer the fragment when a sink reads both.

sources.name: location.href
sources.explain: The full URL read as one string and then parsed in JS (split, substring, regex). Attackers control path, query, and fragment portions.
sources.notes: Reviewers often mis-audit this: code that 'parses the URL itself' with indexOf/split frequently confuses which segment it extracted — test whether the tainted portion is the fragment, query, or a path segment the server normalizes.

sources.name: location.pathname
sources.explain: The URL path segment, controllable when the app serves the same page under arbitrary paths (SPA fallback routes, 404 echo pages, rewrite rules).
sources.notes: Server rewrites decide how much of the path you control — probe with /jlf-trace/ segments and check whether the value reaches the page unencoded; percent-encoded characters in the path are decoded by location.pathname.

sources.name: URLSearchParams
sources.explain: new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('x') — the standard structured way pages extract query parameters before feeding them to sinks.
sources.notes: .get() returns the DECODED value — percent-encoding does not neutralize payloads, it just transports them. Also watch .getAll() and iteration patterns that merge repeated parameters.

sources.name: query-string-manual-parsing
sources.explain: Hand-rolled query parsing (split('&'), split('='), bracket-notation expansion like a[b][c]=v into nested objects) instead of URLSearchParams.
sources.notes: Bracket-expanding parsers are the #1 dependency-free prototype pollution source: ?__proto__[x]=y walks into Object.prototype. Also check duplicate-key and missing-value edge cases — manual parsers rarely match URLSearchParams semantics.

sources.name: postMessage-data
sources.explain: event.data received by a window 'message' listener — any origin can deliver it unless the handler checks event.origin.
sources.notes: Delivered browser-to-browser: no server ever sees the payload, so WAFs are blind. Your PoC is an attacker page that iframes or opens the target and calls postMessage — always verify the origin check is missing or bypassable (endsWith/includes) before claiming exploitability.

sources.name: document.referrer
sources.explain: The Referer of the previous page, read by JS for analytics, theming, or routing decisions.
sources.notes: Attacker-controlled when the victim arrives via a link from the attacker's page (attacker.com/path-payload). Check Referrer-Policy: 'no-referrer' or 'origin' on the LINKING page kills the vector, but the attacker controls their own page's policy — usually fully usable.

sources.name: window.name
sources.explain: A per-tab string that persists across ALL navigations of the tab, including cross-origin ones; any previously visited site can plant it.
sources.notes: Survives cross-origin navigation — attacker page sets window.name then navigates the tab to the target. The target's access log shows a clean request: no query, no fragment. The stealthiest DOM XSS source.

sources.name: localStorage
sources.explain: Persistent origin-wide key-value store read via localStorage.getItem; values planted earlier (by any page on the origin) are re-read on every visit.
sources.notes: Second-order by design: find the WRITE path first (which parameter/API value gets stored), then the READ-into-sink path — the pair is the finding. Survives browser restarts and is shared by every tab on the origin.

sources.name: sessionStorage
sources.explain: Per-tab session-scoped store read via sessionStorage.getItem; planted values survive same-tab navigations (wizard steps, SPA routes).
sources.notes: Tab-isolated: no cross-tab amplification, but perfect for multi-step flows where step 1 stores and step 4 renders. Dies when the tab closes — PoC must stay in one tab.

sources.name: document.cookie
sources.explain: Reading document.cookie returns all non-HttpOnly cookies for the origin as one string; pages parse it in JS for tokens and preferences.
sources.notes: Attacker control comes from cookie-setting vectors: a tainted document.cookie WRITE elsewhere, cookie tossing from a sibling subdomain, or CRLF-free server-set cookies reflecting input. HttpOnly blocks the read — check which cookie is actually consumed.

sources.name: xhr-response
sources.explain: XMLHttpRequest responseText/responseJSON consumed by the page — attacker-influenced when the API reflects stored user data or when the endpoint itself is attacker-controllable.
sources.notes: Stored-XSS carrier: plant the payload via the API (profile field, comment), then it returns in every XHR response. Test response JSON keys for '__proto__' too — merge sinks pollute from parsed responses.

sources.name: fetch-response
sources.explain: fetch().then(r => r.json()) results rendered or merged by the page — same taint profile as XHR but dominant in modern SPAs.
sources.notes: Trace whether the fetched URL itself is attacker-controllable (open redirect/proxy endpoints let you serve fully attacker JSON) — that upgrades reflected data into a fully controlled response body.

sources.name: websocket-message
sources.explain: Messages arriving via WebSocket onmessage — tainted when the server relays other users' input (chat, collaboration) or when the socket endpoint accepts unauthenticated cross-origin connections.
sources.notes: WebSockets are not same-origin restricted — the server must check the Origin header itself; if it does not, YOUR page can open a socket to the target (CSWSH) and both send and receive messages as the victim.

sources.name: broadcastchannel-message
sources.explain: e.data from BroadcastChannel onmessage — posted by ANY same-origin tab, iframe, or worker on the same channel name.
sources.notes: No origin field exists on BroadcastChannel messages — handlers cannot authenticate the sender at all. Any same-origin injection primitive (even a low-severity one) can post to the channel and detonate every open tab.

sources.name: spa-hash-router-param
sources.explain: Route parameters extracted from the fragment by SPA routers (#/user/<param>, #!/search/<term>) and injected into templates or page state.
sources.notes: Router params are the fragment, so they never reach the server — WAF-blind. Check whether the router decodes params (most do) and whether route guards or template bindings sanitize before rendering.

sources.name: indexeddb
sources.explain: Structured client-side database read via IDBObjectStore.get/cursor; stores whole objects cached from APIs or user input.
sources.notes: Second-order like localStorage but stores rich objects — offline-first apps cache entire API responses here, so one poisoned cached record detonates on every offline render. Inspect with DevTools > Application > IndexedDB.

sources.name: dom-form-values
sources.explain: input.value, textarea.value, and form field reads consumed by JS — attacker-controlled when fields are pre-filled from URLs or when the attacker is the one typing (stored/self vectors).
sources.notes: Field NAMES matter too: serializers that expand names like 'a[b]' into nested objects are prototype pollution sources. Pure 'victim types payload into a field' chains are self-XSS — find how the field gets pre-filled remotely.

sources.name: window.opener
sources.explain: Reference to the window that opened the current one; the opener can be re-navigated (reverse tabnabbing) or postMessaged by the opened page, and vice versa.
sources.notes: Links/forms with target=_blank and no rel=noopener leave window.opener set: the opened page can set opener.location to a phishing copy of the origin. Modern browsers imply noopener for target=_blank, but explicit window.open calls and older browsers still expose it.
